notes.b: Work gives a person income, purpose and a place in society, so losing it hits a person's money, status and wellbeing at the same time. These are individual effects, felt by the person who lost the job.
points: Financial insecurity: lost income forces people to cut spending and lower their living standard, and to rely on savings, credit or welfare payments, which are lower than a wage.
Debt: unpaid bills and loans build up, which can lead to mortgage or rent arrears (payments missed) and, in serious cases, repossession of the home or homelessness.
Loss of identity and status: work gives identity, purpose and social standing, so unemployed people may feel undervalued, worthless, a failure or guilty, and lose self-esteem.
Stress, anxiety and depression: long-term unemployment can create feelings of hopelessness, and stress and depression can in turn affect a person's health.
Social isolation: losing work removes daily contact with colleagues, and having less money for leisure reduces participation in social activities.
Loss of daily routine can lead to boredom.
Addiction: some people turn to alcohol, drugs or gambling to cope, which adds to their difficulties.
Loss of skills over time and falling confidence make it harder to get a job, so a person can slip into long-term unemployment.
notes.tip: Name each point as an individual effect and give the reason it follows, for example lost income, so debt. Keep debt and loss of confidence here; arguments at home belong to the family.

notes.b: Young people who cannot find work are at the start of adult life, so unemployment delays the steps that normally follow a first job.
points: Delayed independence: without a wage, a young adult may have to remain at the parental home instead of moving out.
Delay in starting a family or buying a home, because there is no steady income to save or borrow against.
Risk of emigrating in search of work, which takes the young person away from family and friends.
notes.tip: If the question asks about a young adult, use the same answer as for the individual but lean the effects toward young people, as above.

notes.b: When an adult loses a job, the whole household feels it. These are family effects, felt by the people who live together and share the household income.
points: Reduced income lowers the family's standard of living, so it may struggle to afford food, clothing, heating and other household bills, and it relies on welfare payments.
Debt and housing risk: arrears on rent, mortgage or utilities build up, and families that fall behind on rent or mortgage repayments face a risk of losing the home and of homelessness.
Financial pressure, changed roles within the household and the stress of one or both adults being at home cause arguments and strain relationships.
Relationship strain can lead, in some cases, to separation or family breakdown.
Children may have to give up activities such as sports, music lessons or school trips, and may feel different from classmates or be teased.
Family members may emigrate for work, which breaks up the family's support network.
Reliance on welfare payments can shape family finances for long periods.
notes.tip: Arguments and children missing out are family effects, so give them as family points, not individual ones. Examiners need one reference to each level for full marks.

notes.b: Children grow up in the household, so the effects of unemployment can follow them into school and into their own working lives.
points: Children's educational opportunities suffer when a family cannot pay for books, technology or a quiet place to study.
Children of unemployed parents have fewer working role models (people whose working life they can copy), which can lower their expectations of work.
Intergenerational unemployment: children raised in a household with no one in work may come to expect unemployment, so the disadvantage is repeated when they reach working age.
Financial pressure at home can lead to early school leaving, which reduces the qualifications children take into the labour market.
notes.tip: Weak employment role models and intergenerational unemployment are the terms to use when a question asks about the effects on children or on society.

notes.b: Unemployment is also a cost to the whole community and the State, because jobless people stop paying into the system and start drawing on it. These are society effects.
points: Cost to the State: higher spending is needed on social welfare payments and related supports such as medical cards, fuel and housing supports, and taxes may have to rise to pay for it.
Loss of income tax and social insurance (PRSI) income means less money for public services.
Loss of production and skills: the economy's output falls and unused skills are wasted.
Crime, antisocial behaviour and vandalism can follow in areas with high long-term unemployment. This is an association with those areas, not a rule about unemployed people.
Emigration of working-age and skilled workers reduces the population, the skills base and future tax income.
The black economy grows, as unpaid or undeclared work avoids tax and PRSI, so the State loses that income.
Social exclusion and inequality: people cut off from work, income and social networks become harder to reintegrate, and the gap widens between those in work and those without.
Pressure on health and community services: more people use mental health, addiction and counselling services, and local authorities, voluntary bodies and community groups take on more work.
notes.tip: Give crime as something that can follow in areas of high unemployment, not as a certainty. For emigration, say what is lost: people, skills and tax income. Name the effect, then say who bears the cost.

notes.h: Local chain reaction in unemployment black spots
notes.b: A black spot is an area of very high unemployment. When many people in one place lose their jobs, the effects feed on each other and the whole area declines.
points: Falling local spending closes shops and services, which causes further job losses in the area.
Population loss reduces the number of users of local schools and transport, making services harder to keep open, because people move away in search of work.
Black spots acquire a poor reputation, which deters investment and new businesses.
People still in work feel it too: they face job insecurity and fear of redundancy, and where an area empties there is less local demand for their products and services.
notes.tip: Describe local decline as a chain: spending falls, shops close, more jobs go, people leave. Do not repeat the causes of unemployment here.

notes.h: Linking effects across the three levels
notes.b: The levels are connected, and an answer is stronger when it shows how one effect leads to the next.
points: Effects chain from one level to the next: lost income (individual) leads to arrears and strain (family) and, multiplied across a town, to closed shops and falling tax income (society).

The same effect can sit at more than one level, but give it once, at the level the question asks about. For example, depression is an individual effect, while the cost of treating it falls on society.
notes.tip: Give a reason why each effect follows from the one before, for example lost income, so debt.

notes.b: Marks go to answers that cover every level the question names, with each effect named and explained.
points: Cover each level asked for: at least one effect for the individual, the family and society, then further effects.
Give each point a name and a short explanation of why it follows, for example lost income, so debt.
notes.tip: Name the level before each effect and aim for one more effect than the minimum. Do not describe the causes of unemployment; the question asks for effects only.

keyTerms.definition: A lack of secure income that leaves a household unable to meet regular costs.
Missed or late repayments on a mortgage.
A fall in social standing and self-esteem that can follow the loss of work.
A lack of regular contact with other people, often caused by losing work.
Unemployment passed from parents to children, who may lack working role models.
Paid work carried out without being declared for tax or social insurance.
Conduct that harms or disturbs others, such as crime, vandalism or intimidation.
Leaving one's own country to live and work abroad.

factCards.term: Three effects of unemployment on the individual
factCards.definition: Financial insecurity; loss of self-esteem and status; depression.

factCards.term: Four effects of unemployment on the family
factCards.definition: Lower living standard and debt; strain on relationships; children losing activities and educational opportunities; risk of losing the home.

factCards.term: Three effects of unemployment on society
factCards.definition: Higher welfare and tax costs; crime, antisocial behaviour and vandalism, which are associated with areas of high unemployment; emigration of skilled workers.

factCards.term: Local chain reaction in an unemployment black spot
factCards.definition: Falling spending closes shops and services, which causes further job losses and encourages people to leave the area.

factCards.term: How unemployment can pass to the next generation
factCards.definition: Children have fewer working role models and may lower their expectations of work.

questions.prompt: Outline two effects of unemployment on the individual.
questions.model: Financial insecurity: loss of income forces cuts in spending, lower living standards, debt and possible mortgage arrears. Loss of identity and status: the person may feel undervalued and lose self-esteem and social standing. Depression, stress and social isolation: loss of work removes daily contact with others and can create hopelessness and failure. Each effect needs a clear explanation to earn full marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss the effects of unemployment on the family and on society.
questions.model: Family: reduced income and living standard, debt and risk of losing the home; strain on relationships and possible separation; children losing activities and educational opportunities, such as books or a quiet study space; reliance on welfare for long periods. Society: higher welfare and tax costs for the state; loss of tax and PRSI income for public services; crime, antisocial behaviour and vandalism in areas with high long-term unemployment; emigration of workers and skills; growth of the black economy; decline of shops and services in unemployment black spots, which deters investment. Intergenerational effects link the family and society, as disadvantage can be repeated by the next generation.
